text.p: Luxembourg will on Wednesday outline proposals for its 1998 budget, safe in the knowledge the tiny Grand Duchy is one of the few European Union members whose participation in the single currency project is assured.
Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker and cabinet ministers met during the weekend and on Monday to discuss the budget, which will be presented to parliament in September.
No details of their talks have emerged so far.

Luxembourg, home to just 418,000 people, aims for a balanced budget in which spending growth corresponds to the "budgetary standard" or growth norm -- essentially the medium-term growth rate of gross domestic product (GDP).

Budget ministry officials were unavailable to comment on Tuesday, but according to Luxembourg media the standard for 1998 was set at four percent, which implies a spending target of 170 billion Luxembourg francs.
Finance ministry figures show spending in the 1996 and 1997 budgets at 157 and 163 billion francs respectively.

While other EU members struggle to cut public deficits and debt, notably France and Germany, Luxembourg and Finland formed the bloc's star duo last year meeting all the criteria for joining the single currency.
They are expected to do so again this year.
A decision on who takes part in the euro currency union due to be launched on January 1, 1999, will be taken next year based initially on 1997 finances and economic performance.

A recent forecast by Deutsche Bank predicted Luxembourg would continue to boast healthy finances, with a budget surplus to GDP ratio of 1.0 percent in 1997 and 1998, and debt at just 6.6 and 7.0 percent of GDP repectively.
This compares to Maastricht Treaty requirements for joining the euro which call for a deficit/GDP ratio limited to three percent and a debt/GDP ratio of a maximum 60 percent.
In its April annual economic survey the Paris-based OECD think-tank said Luxembourg was not expected to experience any budgetary difficulties in the near future.

However, the rapid rise in government spending could be a problem. In the past this had been met by fast growth in tax revenues, but it was uncertain how long the current buoyancy of corporate tax receipts would continue.
At the same time, the OECD said, limiting spending was difficult, with about two thirds of expenditure directly linked to the consumer price index.
It noted public sector wage increases had been fixed until 1999, and as in the rest of Europe, an ageing population would put increasing demands on the system.
